variants.headline: Bid to remove government fails
variants.sub: The attempt to remove the government by an Assembly vote has failed.
variants.body:
The vote to bring down the government has failed. The result settles that attempt, not every argument about the administration. For {target}, it is important to distinguish survival of a parliamentary challenge from an unlimited endorsement of political conduct or future decisions.

We find the conduct of {target} wanting. Whatever the result of this attempt, parliamentary manoeuvre is no substitute for political responsibility or an adequate account of the public interest.

variants.headline: Confidence challenge falls short
variants.sub: The government has survived a vote intended to bring it down.
variants.body:
Remaining in office and winning every argument are different achievements. The government's opponents have failed to bring it down by a vote in the Assembly. This is the institutional fact against which the conduct of {target} should be considered, without inventing a margin or motive.

We find the conduct of {target} wanting. Whatever the result of this attempt, parliamentary manoeuvre is no substitute for political responsibility or an adequate account of the public interest.

variants.headline: Government survives the Assembly test
variants.sub: A vote to bring down the government has failed in {colony}.
variants.body:
The Assembly challenge has not removed the government. A failed vote is a definite parliamentary outcome, even where the wider political argument remains open. The question for readers considering {target} is what responsible conduct requires after this attempt, rather than what an imagined tally might suggest.

We find the conduct of {target} wanting. Whatever the result of this attempt, parliamentary manoeuvre is no substitute for political responsibility or an adequate account of the public interest.
